node.label: Carolyn Steedman
node.date_label: Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) · Dust (2001) · Labours Lost (2009)
node.description: Carolyn Steedman argued that working-class lives contain desires and conflicts that general accounts of class cannot adequately explain. Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) uses her own and her mother’s histories to question narratives that deny working-class people psychological individuality. Geoff Eley credited reading the book with shaping his intellectual development. Emily Cuming later questioned its occasionally rigid alignment of narrative genres with class experience and read the mother’s choice of a Lowry picture as resistance to the daughter’s interpretation. Dust (2001) examines the surviving matter of history and historians’ engagement with archives. Labours Lost (2009) restores domestic servants’ feelings and self-representations to social history while challenging Thompson’s portrayal of their resignation.
node.representative_figures_and_works: The Tidy House: Little Girls Writing (1982); Landscape for a Good Woman (Virago, 1986; Rutgers edition, 1987); Childhood, Culture and Class in Britain: Margaret McMillan, 1860–1931 (1990); Strange Dislocations (1995); Dust (Manchester, 2001; Rutgers edition, 2002); Master and Servant (2007); Labours Lost (2009); An Everyday Life of the English Working Class (2013).
node.scope_note: Landscape and Dust were read through publisher descriptions and named scholarly readers, not in full. Labours Lost was read at selected publisher-excerpt pages. “Why Clio doesn’t Care” was read only in its journal abstract. “On the Doorstep” was read in full; the underlying correspondence and earlier cited works were not independently read. Selected Eley and Lawrence passages and Cuming’s section iii were read; their complete books/article were not.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Labours Lost (2009), Steedman challenges Thompson’s account of servants’ resignation in “The Crime of Anonymity” (1975), emphasizing short service careers and inventive expressions of resentment.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, pp. 8–9: “not at all fatalistic about their future.” The cited Thompson chapter itself remains unread; this is Steedman’s explicit objection.

proposed_edges.relationship: In A Crooked Line (2005), Eley identifies reading Steedman’s Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) as important to his own encounter with changes in historical thinking.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher chapter 4, printed p. 173: “key part in my own encounter.” Read selected pp. 172–175 and 178–180; no claim about every aspect of Eley’s work.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Inventing the ‘Traditional Working Class’” (2016), Lawrence develops Steedman’s Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) criticism of Young and Willmott’s treatment of mother–daughter relations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge repository manuscript, p. 16, paragraph beginning “But even if,” and note 70 on manuscript p. 37: “guilt and resentment.” Lawrence adds interview evidence unavailable to Steedman; selected passage, not whole article, read.

proposed_edges.relationship: The abstract of “Why Clio doesn’t Care” (1992) presents Steedman’s argument that British women’s history constituted a politics through shared cultural and educational assumptions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Journal abstract, first two sentences: “a politics rather than a theoretical construct.” Body unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: The abstract of “Why Clio doesn’t Care” (1992) uses Steedman’s Margaret McMillan biography (1990) to examine the differing narrative conventions of biography, autobiography and history.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Journal abstract, final two sentences on genre and public political lives. Full article and McMillan book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Labours Lost (2009), Steedman proposes restoring waged domestic workers’ feelings and self-representations to histories of English social structure.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, p. 9: “move out of the big house.” A stated research programme, not verification of all the book’s cases.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “On the Doorstep” (2024), Steedman makes paid archival research and ownership of its products a central question for understanding how history is made.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete institutional article, especially pp. 24–26: “Who does the work in the archive?” Her interpretation of Thompson–Dodd correspondence; underlying archive unread. Dust (2001) not freshly read.
proposed_edges.map_label: Who does and owns archival work?

proposed_edges.relationship: Eley’s A Crooked Line (2005) reads Landscape for a Good Woman (1986) as challenging the gendered working-class narrative offered by Thompson’s The Making of the English Working Class (1963).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Eley, printed p. 173, “counter-counternarrative”; he says the challenge also re-enables Thompson’s narrative. Mediated assessment; Landscape body unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Gendered limits of the class narrative

proposed_edges.relationship: In his review “Desire” (1986), Raymond Williams questions the theoretical development and reading behind the treatment of Marxism in Carolyn Steedman’s Landscape for a Good Woman (1986), while endorsing its broader challenge.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The complete review was read on the magazine’s own site. This paragraph criticises the theoretical treatment of Marxism; the next endorses the challenge to production-centred accounts of consciousness. The edge records a qualified criticism, not wholesale rejection.
